For decades, UN peacekeeping operations have remained amongst the most effective multilateral instruments for preventing and mitigating armed conflict, sustaining peace, and responding to an ever-evolving spectrum of threats to international peace and security. Mr. Chair, peacekeeping remains one of the most visible and valuable expressions of multilateral solidarity. Over the decades, UN peacekeepers have prevented escalation, supported fragile transitions, and protected millions of civilians caught in conflict. Yet, the environment in which peacekeeping operates today is vastly different from when the first mission was deployed. Operations are now called upon to address root causes of instability, manage transitions, and operate alongside regional and bilateral initiatives, often under mandates that are ambitious but resources are limited. The prevailing financial constraints within the United Nations have necessitated drawdowns and force restructurings. This situation undermines the capacity of peacekeeping missions to fulfill their mandates and to protect both peacekeepers and the civilians they serve. The success of peace operations increasingly depends on political goodwill that fosters enhanced cooperation with most host— with the host nations and regional security mechanisms, and ensures that solutions are grounded in local reality, ownership by host communities, and build mutual trust, ultimately enabling peacekeepers to fulfill their mandates effectively. It also depends on a deep understanding of operational environments to enable context-specific missions. One of the recent innovative approaches to context-specific peace operations is the establishment of the Security Council-mandated missions exemplified by the Multinational Security Support Mission in Haiti, which Kenya has had the privilege to lead. These missions serve as strong proof of concept for adaptive and responsive peace operations. Mr. Chair, peacekeeping cannot succeed in isolation. It must be part of a continuum that connects prevention, peacebuilding, and sustainable development. As we look ahead, Kenya proposes 5 broad priorities for the next phase of reform and implementation. First, toward a coherent and flexible mandate. Peacekeeping missions must be grounded in realistic objectives with regular strategic reviews that allow mandates to evolve alongside political realities. The Council, the Secretariat, and and field missions must work in closer concert to ensure coherence between political, humanitarian, and development instruments, from peacekeeping to peacebuilding and recovery. Second, towards stronger partnership and collaboration, where the UN and AU partnership, for example, must be institutionalized through predictable and sustainable financing arrangements consistent with Security Council Resolution 2719. We must also leverage the comparative advantages of regional and sub-regional organizations such as AGAD in mediation, early warning, and preventive diplomacy, and reinforce triangular cooperation between troop-contributing countries, the Security Council and the Secretariat. Third, towards sustainable peace and national ownership, every mission should contribute to building the national institutions that will ultimately sustain peace. Peacekeeping transitions must therefore be planned early and undertaken jointly with national authorities and other relevant stakeholders. The goal must not only be responsible withdrawal, but durable peace dividends for affected populations. Fourth, the foundation of successful future peace operations is comprehensive and forward-looking training. To this end, Kenya continues to collaborate with the UN and partner member states to strengthen peacekeeping by enhancing the training capacities of both our national contingents and peacekeepers from around the world. Such training ensures that peacekeepers are fully prepared to meet the complex challenges of modern operations. Lastly, Kenya believes that sustainable funding coupled with deeper cooperation between United Nations and regional mechanisms such as the Africa Union will be decisive in shaping the next generation of peacekeeping operations, those that are regionally anchored, nationally owned, and strategically aligned with peace building priorities. Mr. Chair, Kenya affirms its steadfast commitment to supporting peacekeeping operations and calls upon the international community to strengthen its solidarity with societies affected by conflict. Addressing the evolving challenges of modern peacekeeping, from technological advancement and resource constraints to complex political dynamics, demands a unified and forward-looking approach. It is only through collection— collective action, innovation, and sustained investment that peacekeeping missions can continue to protect civilians, uphold peace, and foster lasting stability across the globe. Kenya stands ready to work constructively with all member states to build a peacekeeping architecture that is effective, equitable, and enduring. I thank you.
